response.title: how to run a space heater during a power outage
response.answer:
You can run an electric space heater during a power outage, but you'll need an alternative electricity source. The main challenge is that space heaters consume a lot of power, typically 750–1,500 watts.

Your best options

Power source

Practicality




Portable power station (battery)

	

Yes, if rated for 1,500W+ continuous output

	

Safe indoors, but short runtime




Gasoline inverter generator

How long can a battery run a space heater?

Assuming 85% usable energy after inverter losses:

Battery capacity

500 Wh

2,000 Wh

5,000 Wh

Heater power

500W — low-power heater
750W — medium setting
1,500W — full power

Estimated continuous runtime

1.1 hours

(68 minutes)

Illustrative estimate assuming constant heater draw. Actual runtime varies with battery condition, temperature, and inverter efficiency.
What I recommend

For short outages: A portable power station with at least 2,000W continuous AC output can power a typical 1,500W heater, but a 2kWh battery will last only about an hour.

For long outages: A properly sized inverter generator is more practical for continuous electric heating. It must operate outdoors, at least 20 feet from doors, windows, and vents, with exhaust directed away from the house. Never run it in a garage, even with the door open.

For maximum efficiency: Instead of powering an electric space heater, consider battery-powered heated blankets or clothing. These consume dramatically less electricity. Never use an outdoor propane heater, camping stove, charcoal grill, or generator indoors because of carbon monoxide poisoning risks.

Also, plug a space heater directly into a properly rated power source, not a household extension cord or power strip.

You can run an electric space heater during a power outage, but you'll need an alternative electricity source. **The main challenge is that space heaters consume a lot of power**, typically 750–1,500 watts.

## Your best options

| Power source | Can run a 1,500W heater? | Practicality |
|---|---|---|
| Portable power station (battery) | Yes, if rated for 1,500W+ continuous output | Safe indoors, but short runtime |
| Gasoline inverter generator | Yes, with sufficient capacity | Good for extended outages; outdoors only |
| Home backup battery (e.g., Tesla Powerwall) | Yes | Convenient but uses substantial battery capacity |
| Car + inverter | Sometimes, with specialized equipment | Generally impractical for a 1,500W heater |
| UPS for computers | Usually no | Insufficient capacity |

## How long can a battery run a space heater?

Assuming 85% usable energy after inverter losses:

{@body const [capacity,setCapacity] = DIL.useState(2000)}
{@body const [wattage,setWattage] = DIL.useState("1500")}
{@body const hours = capacity*0.85/Number(wattage)}

  <row align="center" justify="between">
    <text color="secondary" size="sm">500 Wh</text>
    <title size="lg" color="default" tabularNums>{capacity.toLocaleString()} Wh</title>
    <text color="secondary" size="sm">5,000 Wh</text>
  </row>
  <slider min={500} max={5000} step={500} value={capacity} onChange={setCapacity}/>
  <text weight="medium">Heater power</text>
  <radio-group direction="col" value={wattage} onChange={setWattage}>
    <radio value="500">500W — low-power heater</radio>
    <radio value="750">750W — medium setting</radio>
    <radio value="1500">1,500W — full power</radio>
  </radio-group>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">Estimated continuous runtime</text>
  <row align="baseline" gap={2}>
    <title size="2xl" color="default" tabularNums>{hours.toFixed(1)} hours</title>
    <text color="secondary" size="sm">({Math.round(hours*60)} minutes)</text>
  </row>
  <box background="surface-tertiary" height="10px" radius="full" clip>
    <box background="rgba(37,99,235,0.85)" width={`${Math.min(hours/8*100,100)}%`} height="100%" radius="full"/>
  </box>
  <caption>Illustrative estimate assuming constant heater draw. Actual runtime varies with battery condition, temperature, and inverter efficiency.</caption>
</box>
